title: Unique matching families on a locally directed family of opens
statement: Let $T$ be a topological space in universe $u$, let $I$ be a universe-$u$ thin category (with arbitrary hom universe), and let $U_i$ be opens with $U_i\subseteq U_j$ for every arrow $i\to j$. Suppose the common lower members cover every intersection $U_i\cap U_j$: every point of this intersection lies in some $U_k$ with arrows $k\to i$ and $k\to j$. Let $P_i$ be sheaves of sets on $T$ (values in universe $\max(u,w)$), with morphisms $r_f:P_j\to P_i$ for arrows $f:i\to j$ such that $r_{g\circ f}=r_f\circ r_g$. Suppose $r_f$ is bijective on sections of every open contained in $U_i$, and restriction $P_i(V)\to P_i(V\cap U_i)$ is bijective for every open $V$. Then for $V\subseteq U_i$ and $x\in P_i(V)$ there is a unique family $s_j\in P_j(V)$ such that $r_f(s_j)=s_k$ for every arrow $f:k\to j$, and $s_i=x$. No covering of all of $T$ or nonempty index set is required.

proof.text: For i,j and V contained in U_i, the opens V intersection U_k, indexed by k admitting arrows to i and j, cover V intersection U_j. Use a subtype of I with nonempty hom propositions so its universe remains u.

Two matching families with the same i component agree on each common lower member. The local bijectivity of r_(k→j) then gives equality of their j components on the covering of V intersection U_j. Sheaf separation and the support restriction bijection give equality on V.

To extend x, on V intersection U_k put the inverse of r_(k→j) applied to r_(k→i)(x restricted). On overlaps refine by lower members mapping to both indices. Composition and thinness identify both restricted formulas; injectivity of the transition makes them equal. The sheaf gluing axiom gives a section over V intersection U_j, which extends uniquely to V by the support bijection.

The local formula for each extended j component implies all transition equations after refinement; thinness identifies the two composites to the same upper member. Applying the formula to two identity arrows and cancelling the bijective transition shows the i component is x. The previously proved uniqueness completes the claim.
